r411: The Pastor Nobody Seemed to Listen To
r412: Samuel, 52, pastor of a small church in Kottayam, Kerala
r413: Pastor Samuel Thomas has led a small church in Kottayam for eleven years. Lately attendance has dropped, two elders openly criticise his preaching in WhatsApp groups, and a family he once helped through a crisis now walks past him without greeting. When he proposed a new youth programme, the committee voted it down in four minutes. At home he lies awake replaying every remark. On Sundays he notices he has started preaching to win the critics rather than to feed the people. His wife says he snaps at the children. He prays, but the prayers sound like complaints. One night he tells her, "Maybe God has finished with me here. Nobody listens anymore." He feels foolish, angry and deeply hurt all at once.
r414: For a leader, open criticism can register in the brain much like a physical threat. Studies suggest social rejection activates some of the same regions involved in processing pain. Samuel's alarm system, the amygdala, kept firing at night, and stress hormones made his rumination worse. Underneath sat an older belief. As the eldest son of a strict father, he learned that love came through performance. So the congregation's disapproval felt like a verdict on his worth, not just feedback on a programme. When identity rests on approval, a leader either fights for control or collapses inward. Samuel was doing both, preaching defensively by day and shrinking by night.
r415: A retired pastor friend asked him one question over chai. "Whose approval did you need before you ever became a pastor?" Samuel cried in the car afterwards. He began to see that his call came from God, not from the committee, and that he could listen to criticism without letting it rename him.
r416: Write down why God called him, to separate the call from the applause
r417: Calm the body before replying to any criticism
r418: Meet the two elders one by one to listen, not to defend
r419: Ask what is true in the criticism and change that part
r420: Keep serving the people who are still there with joy
r421: Find a mentor outside the church to talk to honestly
r422: Jesus was often not respected. In His home town "he could there do no mighty work" and He "marvelled because of their unbelief" (Mark 6:5-6). Yet He did not lose His identity, because before any ministry began the Father had said, "Thou art my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Mark 1:11). Paul faced critics in Corinth who mocked his speaking. He wrote, "with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you... he that judgeth me is the Lord" (1 Corinthians 4:3-4). Moses, criticised by his own brother and sister, stayed meek and let God defend him (Numbers 12:3). Leaders are called to serve, not to be admired, and to entrust their reputation to God.
r423: God made us for belonging, so rejection hurts. That pain is not weakness. It is a sign we were wired for love. But God also designed the brain so that identity can be anchored in a secure relationship. When we repeatedly rest in the Father's love, the calming pathways between the prefrontal cortex and the alarm system appear to grow stronger. A secure leader can hear hard words without being flooded. Then the thinking brain stays online, and he can listen, learn and stay kind. Security in God frees us to serve people instead of needing them.

r428: Samuel met both elders. One softened and admitted he was grieving his own son leaving the church. The other stayed cold and later left. Attendance did not suddenly rise. But Samuel slept better, preached more freely and started a small youth Bible study in his home, which grew to fourteen. He still feels the sting of criticism, but it no longer decides his worth.
r429: A leader who is secure in God's love can hear criticism without being destroyed by it.
r430: When people don't like what you do, God still loves you, so you can listen and keep doing good.
r431: The Young Manager and the Senior Staff
r432: Ananya, 29, newly promoted manager at a logistics company in Hyderabad
r433: Ananya Reddy was promoted to lead a team of nine at a logistics company in Hyderabad. Five of them are older men who have worked there for over fifteen years. In meetings they talk over her, call her "baby madam" when she leaves the room, and quietly go to her own boss about decisions she has already made. One senior, Mr Rao, simply ignores her emails. Ananya overcorrects. Some days she is overly sweet and brings snacks to win them over. Other days she sends sharp messages in capital letters. Neither works. She starts arriving at seven to prove herself and leaving at ten at night. She tells her sister, "Maybe they are right. Maybe I am too young for this."
r434: When we feel disrespected, the brain's threat system reads it as a loss of status and safety. In studies, perceived unfairness and status threat raise stress hormones and narrow our thinking. That explains Ananya's swing between pleasing and controlling, the fawn and fight responses. Underneath was an impostor feeling. She grew up being told that girls should be quiet and never argue with elders. So when older men resisted her, an old rule fired inside, "You have no right to lead them." The senior staff also carried their own fear, of being replaced, overlooked or made irrelevant by someone young.
r435: A mentor told her, "Respect is partly given, partly earned and partly negotiated. You are trying to earn it by exhausting yourself." Ananya decided to stop chasing approval and start building relationships, with clear expectations and real curiosity about her team.
r436: Meet each senior one to one and ask what they know that she does not
r437: Name the problem calmly and privately, with one clear request
r438: Honour their experience openly in front of the team
r439: Agree with her own boss that decisions go through her
r440: Follow through on every agreement, every time
r441: Leave work on time twice a week to protect her health
r442: Paul told young Timothy, "Let no man despise thy youth, but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity" (1 Timothy 4:12). He did not tell Timothy to demand respect, but to live in a way that would earn it. He also said, "Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father" (1 Timothy 5:1). Honour and authority can go together. Jesus taught that the greatest among us is the one who serves (Luke 22:26). And Esther, a young woman placed in a hard role, was reminded that she had come to her position "for such a time as this" (Esther 4:14).
r443: God made people to cooperate in groups, and the brain is finely tuned to fairness and respect. When a leader gives honour first, it can lower others' sense of threat and make them more open. When she stays calm, her steady nervous system helps calm the room, a process called co-regulation. God also designed courage to grow through practice. Each calm, clear conversation strengthens new pathways, so the next one feels a little easier. Authority that serves is how God intended leadership to work.
r444: 1 Timothy 4:12|Let no man despise thy youth, but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
r448: Two of the seniors warmed up within a month. Mr Rao stayed difficult, and Ananya had to document a missed deadline and involve HR, which she hated doing. But she held steady and stayed respectful. Six months later Mr Rao asked her advice on a client problem. She still has days when she feels too young, but she no longer works fourteen hours a day to prove she belongs.
r449: Respect grows when a leader honours others, sets clear expectations and stops chasing approval.
